newsitem.title: FRANCE: Franco/German EMU statement seen calming mkts now.
newsitem.headline: Franco/German EMU statement seen calming mkts now.

text.p: A Franco/German statement on Thursday reaffirming commitment to a single currency would probably succeed in calming markets for now but was unlikely to erase simmering doubts about EMU, analysts said.
"Statements like this have tended to be reassuring," said Sonja Gibbs, market strategist at Nomura International.
"It won't make things worse, but it isn't going to make the problem go away."
The statement, issued in Paris and Bonn, said Prime Minister Alain Juppe and Chancellor Helmut Kohl spoke by telephone on the afternoon of November 21.

During their conversation, "They reaffirmed France and Germany's commitment to launch Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) within the timetable and criteria fixed by the (Maastricht) treaty," the statement said.
"The prime minister and the chancellor noted that the current exchange rate between the franc and the mark corresponded to the fundamentals of the two national economies," the statement added.

The statement was meant to answer a call on Wednesday from ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing calling for a weaker franc, economists said, and was meant to show markets that France and Germany would not abandon their push for EMU.
"This is a direct response to Giscard," said Cyril Beuzit, bond strategist at Banque Nationale de Paris. "They are denying all rumours of a change in direction or policy."
The statement from Juppe's office said Kohl and Juppe also stated the current franc-mark exchange rate was in line with economic fundamentals in both countries.

Giscard d'Estaing called in a magazine article for a sharp depreciation in the franc against the dollar, implying a similar big fall against the mark, to revive growth and employment. His comments have slightly weakened the franc against the mark.
